content: The chain of survival consists of a sequence of critical actions that, when executed promptly and effectively, significantly reduce the likelihood of death from cardiac arrest. Like a physical chain, its overall strength depends on the integrity of each individual link. The four essential and interconnected components of the chain of survival are early access to emergency services, early initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), early defibrillation, and early provision of advanced medical care. The term chain of survival was first introduced as a slogan during the 1988 Conference on Citizen CPR. It was later featured in an editorial in the Journal of Emergency Medical Services (JEMS) in August 1989 and appeared in the inaugural issue of Currents in Emergency Cardiac Care in 1990. The concept was further developed and formalized in the American Heart Association's 1992 guidelines for cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency cardiac care. Subsequently, the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) endorsed the concept in 1997. The first link, early access, requires that someone witnesses the cardiac arrest and promptly activates the emergency medical services (EMS) system by calling 9-1-1 or the local emergency number. This step is critical to initiating the chain of survival. The second link, early CPR, involves the immediate initiation of bystander CPR following the collapse of the patient. High-quality CPR, performed correctly, can sustain the heart in a state of ventricular fibrillation (VF) for an additional 10 to 12 minutes, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful defibrillation and survival. The third link, early defibrillation, is particularly crucial because most adults who can be successfully resuscitated from cardiac arrest are in ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Early defibrillation is the intervention most strongly associated with improved survival rates. Public access to defibrillation programs, which make automated external defibrillators (AEDs) widely available, can significantly enhance survival outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest scenarios. However, the effectiveness of this link depends on the success of the preceding links in the chain. The fourth and final link, early advanced care, involves the administration of advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) by trained paramedics or other healthcare professionals. In communities with survival rates exceeding 20%, at least two rescuers are typically trained to an advanced level of care. Depending on the country, advanced EMS care may be delivered by paramedics, nurses, physicians, or other qualified personnel.
